blocks.en: The Geometry of LLM-as-Judge: Why Inter-LLM Consensus Is Not
Sourabrata MukherjeeHamna HamnaKalika BaliSunayana SitaramMicrosoft Researcht-somukherje@microsoft.com

LLM judges now score most open-ended NLPoutput, and their mutual agreement is routinelyread as evidence that the scores can be trusted.That reading is unsafe: judges may agree be-cause they capture quality, or because theyshare the same blind spots, and agreementstatistics alone cannot tell these apart. We de-velop a geometric test that can. Treating eachjudge’s scores as a vector, we measure spread,eﬀective rank, the angle to human scores, andthe judge–judge, judge–human, and human–human agreement triple for 42 judges on twocommunity-built Indic benchmarks coveringfour domains and eight languages. Every com-parison is reference-matched: a judge and aheld-out rater are scored against the same two-rater mean, since an averaged reference other-wise ﬂatters judges by several degrees. On sub-jective rubrics, judges agree with one anotheras much as humans do yet reach only 58–66%of human agreement: consensus on an axis hu-mans do not weight. On the one rubric with averiﬁable answer, most of that gap closes. En-sembles converge on the judges’ shared axisrather than the human one, and training widensscores without rotating them. Inter-judge agree-ment is evidence of human alignment only afterthis check passes.1

LLMs are now the default raters for open-ended text(Zheng et al., 2023; Chiang and Lee, 2023; Duboiset al., 2023). They track people closely when arubric has a checkable answer, and far less closelyon the subjective, multilingual, culturally situatedjudgements that dominate real deployments (Wanget al., 2024; Liu et al., 2023; Hada et al., 2024;Watts et al., 2024). Across meta-evaluations, one
lopsided pattern recurs: judges agree strongly withone another while agreeing only weakly with peo-ple (Hada et al., 2024; Watts et al., 2024). How

that pattern is read decides evaluation practice. Ifjudges agree because they capture quality, ensem-bling them is sound and human annotation can bescaled back; if they agree because they share a blindspot, ensembling ampliﬁes the error exactly wherehuman judgement is scarcest. Agreement statis-tics cannot separate the two readings, because bothproduce the same numbers (Calderon et al., 2025).

We separate them by measuring the shape of thedisagreement rather than its size. Suppose humanjudgement varies along many independent aspectsof quality, while each judge’s scores move along afew, largely shared directions (Schütze, 1992; Aroraet al., 2018; Raghu et al., 2017). Judges built onoverlapping pre-training corpora and similar post-training objectives (Ouyang et al., 2022; Bai et al.,2022) are exactly where this should occur, and ityields a prediction that agreement scores cannottest: judge and human scores should sit at a wideangle in score space, and averaging more judgesshould not close it. Throughout, “subspace,” “axis,”and “projection” name patterns in the scores weobserve, never computation inside a model.

We test this prediction on two community-builtIndic benchmarks: real-world cultural QA(Watts et al., 2024), with eight Indic languages,three domains, and three independent raters peritem, and community-health (Hamna et al., 2026;Bhat et al., 2025), judged by 14 base LLMs and27 trained variants of three open families (Brownet al., 2020; Rafailov et al., 2023). One measure-ment choice carries much of the weight. A judgecompared against the average of several raters hasan easier target than a rater compared against asingle colleague, and the diﬀerence is worth sev-eral degrees; wherever we compare a judge with aperson, we therefore hold out one rater and scoreboth against the remaining two. Under this matchedcomparison the prediction holds. On every subjec-tive rubric, judges agree with each other about asmuch as people do while reaching only 58–66% of

Contributions.This paper contributes: (1) a re-porting frame that separates judge–judge, judge–human, and human–human agreement on a matchedreference, with the geometric account scoped as adiagnostic over observed scores (Sec. 3); (2) fourscore-space diagnostics, validated by permutation,FDR, ordinal, human-reference, self-preference,and split-half controls that the collapse pattern sur-vives (Sec. 5.4); (3) a falsiﬁable boundary: a dimen-sionality computed from human raters alone, beforeany LLM is run, predicts which regime a rubricfalls in, with rank necessary and orientation deci-sive; (4) an anatomy of repair, showing that trainingrestores spread rather than orientation and that en-sembling converges on the judges’ shared axis; and(5) a complete release that reproduces every num-ber in this paper with one command (App. O). Agap to human judgement survives every trainingstage we tried, so multi-perspective human ratingremains necessary.

LLM-as-judge was adopted because it tracks hu-mans on open-ended generation (Chiang and Lee,2023; Zheng et al., 2023; Kocmi and Federmann,2023; Dubois et al., 2023), and the reliability litera-ture documented where it does not: ﬂuency and ver-bosity bias, self-preference, and degradation on non-English and culturally situated content (Wang et al.,2024; Zheng et al., 2023; Hada et al., 2024; Wattset al., 2024; Hershcovich et al., 2022). Calderonet al. (2025) argue that agreement statistics alonecannot separate a reliable judge from a plausibleone. Our alternative is diagnostic: rather than askhow large the LLM–human gap is, we ask whatshape it has, and show the shape predicts whenconsensus may be trusted.

Consensus is where this matters most. Ensembleand panel protocols treat inter-judge agreement asreliability (Zheng et al., 2023), assuming averagingcancels idiosyncratic bias. That fails if judges sharethe bias: models trained on overlapping corporawith similar post-training objectives (Ouyang et al.,2022; Bai et al., 2022) can covary strongly whilejointly missing a human-weighted direction. Wemake that failure measurable, and show ensembling
converges on the cohort’s own axis (Sec. 5.6).

Our instruments come from representationalanalysis: principal angles and canonical correlation(Björck and Golub, 1973; Knyazev and Argentati,2002; Raghu et al., 2017), applied to scores ratherthan activations, which keeps the analysis model-agnostic and usable on closed APIs at the cost of adiagnostic rather than mechanistic lens (Sec. 3).

The setting is Indic NLP, a testbed for cross-lingual judge reliability (Watts et al., 2024; Hadaet al., 2024). Our benchmarks supply complemen-tary halves of what the diagnostics need: real-world cultural QA (Watts et al., 2024) givesthree independent raters per item, which makes ahuman ﬂoor measurable at all, while community-health (Hamna et al., 2026; Bhat et al., 2025) givesjudge breadth. We evaluate four standard repairs(Brown et al., 2020; Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailovet al., 2023; Hu et al., 2022; Platt, 1999; Guo et al.,2017); new here is the decomposition (Sec. 5.8)separating ampliﬁcation of a judge’s ranking fromrotation toward humans.

This section deﬁnes what the paper measures. Itis a diagnostic lens over observed scores: “projec-tion,” “subspace,” and “axis” refer to structure inobserved score covariance, never to internal LLMcomputation. Every analysis operates on per-judgescore matrices SJ ∈Rn×m (n items, m rubrics;columns mean-centered). The eight analysed languages(Bengali, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi,Odia, Tamil, Telugu) span Indo-Aryan and Dravid-ian families; DLQ’s comparative split (which addsGujarati and Punjabi) is excluded from analysis (asingle LLM judge with a label-orientation artefact;App. M) and counted only in event totals.

Every QA pair is scored under two paradigms.Standalone: per-rubric ordinal scores over foursubjective CH rubrics (clarity, helpfulness, accu-racy, completeness) plus three DLQ rubrics: taskquality (the single objective rubric: veriﬁable taskconstraints), linguistic acceptability, and hallucina-tions (Chiang and Lee, 2023; Watts et al., 2024).Comparative: judges pick the better of two an-swers. The paradigms separate calibration fromrank-ordering failures (Zheng et al., 2023; Liuet al., 2023); deﬁnitions and verbatim prompts inApp. G, I.

Measurement and inference.Per (judge, rubric,language, domain, eval type) slice we compute theSec. 3 diagnostics: the agreement triple (quadratic-weighted κ in App. M); Cohen’s κ (Cohen, 1960) oncomparative panels; σJ /σH; r95; and θ against thematched human ﬂoor and permutation null (App. L).The training analysis uses a paired item bootstrap(Efron, 1979), B = 1000 over the 405 core itemswith rows reused across (family, stage); with n=3trainable families the smallest one-sided Wilcoxon(Wilcoxon, 1945) p is 0.125, so Wilcoxon is only adirectional summary.
Four analyses plus controls test the geometric ac-count: agreement, boundary, geometry, controls(testing P1–P6; Sec. 5.4), and training.

One construction per comparison.Two conven-tions govern every number below, since mixingthem is the easiest way to manufacture a result. (i)All three legs of an agreement triple are pairwise(rater vs. rater): correlating a judge with the mean ofthree raters gives it a less noisy target than the othertwo legs face, which on task quality alone movesrlh from 0.418 to 0.519 and would lift judges abovethe human ﬂoor. (ii) Every angle compared witha human ﬂoor is reference-matched: one rater isheld out and the mean of the other two is the singlereference that this rater and each judge are scoredagainst. On real-world cultural QA’s subjective rubricsthe three legs separate cleanly: judges agree witheach other about as much as humans agree with eachother (rll 0.356 vs. rhh 0.357 on linguistic accept-ability; 0.349 vs. 0.364 on hallucinations) whileagreeing with humans far less (0.207, 0.239, i.e.58% and 66% of the inter-human level). Match-ing inter-human consensus without matching inter-human agreement is the paper’s central observation:consensus is reached on a diﬀerent axis. The col-lapse is strongest on community-health (41–64%of inter-LLM across four rubrics), and its compar-ative split sharpens it in preference space: LLM–LLM κ = 0.445 vs. LLM–human κ = 0.128, a3.5× gap (base judges, 2, 430 pairs, three-class κ).Table 1A gives the full triple and the matched an-gles; Fig. 2 maps every cell’s gap.

The strongest reading of consensual blindness, thatLLM judges are generically unreliable, is falsiﬁedby real-world cultural QA: with the same items,the same ﬁve judges (deepseek-r1, gpt-4, grok-4,mistral-large-3, llama-3.3-70b), and the same threehumans, task quality lifts LLM–human agreementto 0.418, or 88% of the inter-human level (0.474),against 58% and 66% on the two subjective rubrics.The angle tells the same story with the referencematched: judges sit 60.7◦from the two-rater ref-erence where a held-out human sits 56.4◦, a gapof 4.3◦, against 11.0◦and 9.3◦on the subjectiverubrics. The best single judge (55.3◦) is inside thehuman ﬂoor on task quality; on both subjectiverubrics the best judge (67.3◦, 70.8◦) remains welloutside it. Nor is compression merely cautious scale use:Spearman tracks Pearson to within 0.02 per rubric,and monotone remapping onto the human marginalmoves angles by ≤0.13◦(DLQ) / ≤0.31◦(CH), sojudges occupy a different direction, not a narrowerstretch. The regimes also separate before any LLM is run(P5). The participation ratio dR (Eq. 1), computedfrom the three human raters alone, tracks the LLM–human angle across the nine DLQ rubric×domaincells (ρ = 0.68, p = 0.042, R2 = 0.83, leave-one-cell-out stable). The relation is between regimes,not graded within them: objective cells cluster atdR ≈2.1 and ≈60◦, subjective at ≈2.4 and ≈74◦,while inside the six subjective cells the correlationvanishes (ρ = −0.03). We read dR as a two-regimeseparator, not a dose–response curve, and quote noslope; with three raters it is capped at 3, measuringrater disagreement at this panel size (see Limita-tions). The supported claim is the useful one: aquantity computable from humans alone tells youwhich regime a rubric is in.

Self-preference is not the driver either. Two ofCH’s three answer generators (sarvam-m, qwen3)also serve as judges, and sarvam-m supplies theheadline calibrated judge, so family favouritismcould manufacture the training result. Within a(language, question) triple, a judge’s standardiseddeviation from its triple mean, minus the human’sand then the rest of the cohort’s, isolates familypreference from item diﬃculty and real quality dif-ferences. No family shows an eﬀect (|∆| ≤0.035SD; permutation p ≥0.58; App. M.8).

The geometric account is a diagnostic abstractionover observed score covariance, not a mechanisticclaim about LLM internals (Sec. 3): we cannot tellwhether judges fail to perceive human-weighted di-mensions or perceive but down-weight them, andlabel noise, item ambiguity, and pretraining fa-miliarity remain compatible explanations of theobjective–subjective boundary, so our claim is pre-dictive rather than causal. M.7The dR regression: cells, stability, andentanglement

Across the nine cells (Fig. 15): Spearman ρ =0.68 (p = 0.042; one-sided label-permutationp = 0.0231 over 20,000 permutations), Pearsonr = 0.91, R2 = 0.83. Leave-one-cell-out: ρ ∈[0.55, 0.90], R2 ∈[0.78, 0.94]: no single cell car-ries the result.

The relation is between-regime, not graded.Pearson (0.91) far exceeding Spearman (0.68) isthe tell, and the within-group statistics conﬁrm it:across the six subjective cells alone ρ = −0.03,and the three objective cells show no usable trend(n=3). What the regression detects is the separation

between an objective cluster (dR ≈2.1, θ ≈60◦)and a subjective one (dR ≈2.4, θ≈74◦), not a dose–response curve inside either. We therefore reportdR as a regime separator and quote no degrees-per-dimension slope: ﬁtting one over a dR range of2.10–2.52, four tenths of a single dimension, invitesan extrapolation the data cannot support.
The measure is capped by the panel size.With three raters the participation ratio of an

items×raters matrix cannot exceed 3, so dR mea-sures the dimensionality of rater disagreement asthree raters can express it, not the intrinsic dimen-sionality of the human quality manifold. A largerpanel would be needed for the latter, and wouldlikely shift the absolute values; what a three-raterpanel does support is the ordering, and that is allwe use.

Entanglement caveat. At n=9 cells, dR, inter-rater agreement, and label entropy are tightly cou-pled facets of human disagreement; agreement andentropy each predict the angle about as strongly(ρ = −0.78, −0.80), and rank-based partial corre-lations show the dR signal does not survive con-ditioning on rater agreement (partial ρ = −0.46)and shrinks under conditioning on entropy (partialρ = 0.12). The supported claim is therefore pre-dictive, not causal, and coarse rather than ﬁne: aquantity computable from human raters alone, be-fore any LLM is run, tells you which regime a rubricis in. M.10Ensembling: how far can averaging go?

An ensemble mean must be read against a humanreference built the same way. Scoring a k-judgemean against the three-rater human mean whilescoring a human against a single colleague com-pares an averaged quantity with an unaveraged one,and on that mismatched pairing the ﬁve-judge en-semble appears to sit below the human ﬂoor on allthree rubrics, which would say that ﬁve LLMs ap-proximate the human consensus better than one hu-man does. On the matched construction, where theheld-out human and the ensemble are both scoredagainst the same two-rater mean, the picture re-verses on exactly the rubrics the paper’s thesis con-cerns; Table 3 gives the curve.
Two readings follow. First, ensembling is gen-uinely useful: it buys 7.6–9.5◦between one judgeand ﬁve. Second, what it buys is variance reductiontoward the cohort’s dominant axis, not a new direc-

tion: the k=5 angles land within ∼3.5◦of the co-hort PC1-to-human angles (47.7/64.3/65.5◦), andthe extrapolated limits (66.5◦, 64.6◦) remain out-side the subjective ﬂoors (64.4◦, 63.8◦). Where theshared axis misses the human axis, averaging morejudges from the same cohort converges to the miss.On CH the ensemble reaches 77.6–80.9◦, far out-side anything the single merged reference can becompared against.

We ﬂag one asymmetry that runs against us andis worth stating: even in the matched constructionthe ensemble averages ﬁve judges while the humanside is a single rater. The subjective-rubric conclu-sion therefore holds despite giving the ensemble theadvantage, and the objective-rubric crossing is cor-respondingly easier to achieve than the table makesit look.

The paper uses four angle constructions, which sitat systematically diﬀerent magnitudes for the samecohort. Two axes vary independently: what is com-pared (one rubric vector, a whole subspace, or thecohort’s dominant axis) and against which refer-ence (a single rater, a two-rater mean, or a three-rater mean). Body claims ﬁx both. Table 4 gives thefour constructions side by side; the per-constructionreading of “what it measures” is as follows. The per-rubric matched construction isolates one rubric’sscore direction with judge and held-out human onthe same target. The three-rater-mean variant is thesame comparison, except the judge gets a less noisytarget than any individual human does. The per-judge stacked statistic reports the worst-matcheddirection pair between the two 95%-energy sub-spaces; the cohort stacked variant does the samefor the judges pooled into one subspace rather thanany single judge. The cohort PCA axis reports thealignment of the judges’ best shared direction. Hu-man counterparts exist only on DLQ, which hasthree raters; CH merges its annotators into a singlereference, so no ﬂoor is measurable there and CHnumbers are never compared with one.

The orderings are forced, not accidental: thestacked statistic is the largest principal angle, i.e.,the worst-aligned pair of directions once each side’s95%-energy basis is taken, so it upper-bounds thepicture; the cohort-PCA angle takes the judges’ sin-gle dominant axis, the best-case direction, so itlower-bounds it; per-rubric angles sit in betweenbecause each rubric mixes the judge’s aligned dom-inant component with its misaligned remainder.Concretely, on DLQ task quality the judges’ bestshared direction is well aligned (47.7◦), each rubricvector moderately so (60.7◦), while the full sub-spaces still contain directions nearly orthogonal tothe human ones (84.3–88.9◦stacked), as do the hu-mans’ own (73.9–78.1◦): high stacked angles alonedo not distinguish judges from humans, which iswhy every headline contrast is drawn within oneconstruction against its own matched human refer-ence or permutation null.
